urgency.title: Fake Urgency
urgency.what: The message tries to scare you into acting immediately — saying your account will be blocked in 24 hours, or you must respond right now.
urgency.why: Scammers know that if you panic, you stop thinking clearly. By creating a fake deadline, they stop you from asking family or friends, and push you into making a mistake quickly.
urgency.do: Stop. Breathe. A real bank or government office will NEVER block your account without sending you an official letter or registered notice first. Call the organisation directly on their official number — never the one in the message.

money.title: Money Demand
money.what: The message asks you to send money, pay a fee, or make a transfer — often calling it a 'registration fee', 'processing charge', or 'advance payment'.
money.why: This is the goal of almost every scam. Scammers invent reasons for you to send a small amount first, then disappear with it. Legitimate services never ask for upfront cash to unlock winnings or benefits.
money.do: Never send money to someone you have not verified in person. If it is a real prize or refund, you never need to pay to receive it. Report the message to the National Cyber Crime portal (cybercrime.gov.in).

kyc.title: Fake KYC Request
kyc.what: The message claims your KYC is incomplete or expired, and threatens to block your bank account or mobile number unless you update your details immediately.
kyc.why: Banks and telecom companies do occasionally ask for KYC updates — which is why scammers copy that language exactly. But the real process always happens through the bank's official app, branch, or verified website — never through a link in an SMS.
kyc.do: Go to your bank's official website or app directly. Call the number on the back of your debit card. Never click a link in an SMS and never share your Aadhaar, PAN, OTP, or account number with anyone who contacts you first.

prize.title: Fake Prize or Lottery
prize.what: The message says you have won a large amount of money, a phone, or a prize in a lucky draw — even though you never entered any contest.
prize.why: You cannot win a contest you never entered. This trick works because people want to believe they are lucky. Once you engage, scammers ask for a 'tax fee' or 'processing charge' before releasing your prize — which never arrives.
prize.do: Ignore and delete the message. You have won nothing. Real lotteries in India are rare, regulated, and you must have bought a ticket. If someone calls to 'confirm your prize', hang up.

refund.title: Fake Refund or Cashback
refund.what: The message claims a refund or cashback has been approved for you, and asks you to click a link or scan a QR code to collect it.
refund.why: Scammers exploit the fact that many people have genuine pending refunds. By making you click a link or scan a payment QR, they actually drain money from your account rather than adding to it.
refund.do: Check your refund status through the official app or website only. Remember: to receive a refund or cashback, you should NEVER need to scan a QR code or enter your card or bank details.

threats.title: Fake Legal Threat
threats.what: The message threatens police action, an FIR, a court notice, arrest, or an income tax case against you — unless you call a number or pay immediately.
threats.why: Fear is a powerful tool. Scammers impersonate police, CBI, income tax officers, or cybercrime departments. Real agencies never contact you via SMS or WhatsApp to threaten immediate arrest.
threats.do: Real legal notices are sent by post or through a court process. If you receive a suspicious legal threat, call your local police station directly or visit cybercrime.gov.in. Do not call any number in the message.

personal_info.title: Personal Information Request
personal_info.what: The message asks you to share your OTP, PIN, CVV, card number, bank account number, Aadhaar, or password.
personal_info.why: These are the master keys to your money and identity. No legitimate bank, government office, or company will ever ask for your OTP or password — they already have your account details.
personal_info.do: NEVER share your OTP with anyone, for any reason — even if they claim to be from your bank. Your bank will never ask for it. Hang up immediately if someone asks.

suspicious_link.title: Suspicious Link in Message
suspicious_link.what: The message contains a clickable link — often shortened or disguised — that it urges you to open.
suspicious_link.why: Scam links lead to fake websites that look identical to real banks or companies. Once there, they steal your login details or install malware on your device.
suspicious_link.do: Do not click any link in an unexpected message. If you need to visit a website, type the address directly into your browser. A real bank will never ask you to click an SMS link to log in.

url_shortener.title: Shortened Link (Destination Hidden)
url_shortener.what: The link uses a URL shortener (like bit.ly or tinyurl.com) which hides where it actually takes you.
url_shortener.why: Scammers use link shorteners specifically to hide the real destination — which is usually a phishing website or malware page. You cannot tell where a shortened link goes before clicking it.
url_shortener.do: Never click a shortened link from an unknown sender. If you must check, use a link-preview service to see the destination first. Assume all unexpected shortened links are dangerous.

url_ip_host.title: IP Address Instead of Website Name
url_ip_host.what: Instead of a normal website name like 'sbi.co.in', this link uses a raw IP address like '192.168.1.1'. No real company does this.
url_ip_host.why: Scammers use IP addresses because they are cheap to set up, anonymous, and do not require a domain name registration. Legitimate companies always have a proper website address.
url_ip_host.do: Treat any link with an IP address as dangerous. Do not open it. Real banks and companies always use named domains.

url_at_sign.title: @ Sign Trick in URL
url_at_sign.what: This link contains an '@' symbol — a browser trick where everything before the @ is ignored and you actually go to the address after it.
url_at_sign.why: A link like 'sbi.co.in@evil-scam.com' looks like it goes to SBI, but actually takes you to 'evil-scam.com'. This is a well-known phishing trick.
url_at_sign.do: Any link with '@' in the address bar is a red flag. Do not click it. Copy the part after the @ to see the real destination.

url_punycode.title: Disguised International Characters
url_punycode.what: This link uses 'punycode' — a technical way to register domain names with foreign-looking characters that appear identical to normal letters.
url_punycode.why: Scammers register domains like 'pаypal.com' where the 'а' is a Cyrillic character, not a Latin 'a'. To your eyes, it looks identical to the real site.
url_punycode.do: Look for 'xn--' in the link address — that is the giveaway. Do not visit these sites. Always type trusted website addresses manually.

url_too_many_subs.title: Too Many Sub-domains
url_too_many_subs.what: The link has an unusually large number of dot-separated parts (sub-domains), like 'sbi.login.kyc.verify.evil.com'.
url_too_many_subs.why: Scammers add fake company names as sub-domains to make the URL look legitimate. The real domain is the last two parts — 'evil.com' in this example — which is what matters.
url_too_many_subs.do: Look at the last two parts of the domain name (before the path) to find the real website. If you do not recognise it, do not visit.

url_very_long.title: Unusually Long Link
url_very_long.what: This link is much longer than normal — often over 100 characters with many parameters and codes.
url_very_long.why: Very long links are used to hide important clues in the middle or end, or to carry malicious parameters. Real website links are usually short and readable.
url_very_long.do: Be extra careful with very long links from unknown senders. Check the domain name at the beginning of the link carefully.

url_no_https.title: No Security Encryption (HTTP)
url_no_https.what: This link uses 'http://' instead of 'https://'. The 's' stands for secure — without it, your data is unprotected.
url_no_https.why: Any information you type on an insecure (http) page — like your password or OTP — can be intercepted by anyone on the same network. Real banking and payment websites always use https.
url_no_https.do: Never enter any personal information on a page that starts with http:// instead of https://. Look for the padlock icon in your browser address bar.

url_suspicious_tld.title: Suspicious Domain Extension
url_suspicious_tld.what: This link ends with an unusual extension like .xyz, .top, .icu, .club, or .tk instead of the common .com, .in, .co.in, .gov.in.
url_suspicious_tld.why: These domains are extremely cheap or free, which is why scammers prefer them. Legitimate Indian banks and companies use .co.in, .com, .gov.in, or .org.in.
url_suspicious_tld.do: Be very cautious about any financial or government website that does not use a standard, trusted domain extension. When in doubt, search for the official website rather than clicking the link.

url_many_hyphens.title: Too Many Hyphens in the Address
url_many_hyphens.what: The website address contains multiple hyphens — like 'sbi-kyc-login-secure-portal.in'. Real websites almost never need this.
url_many_hyphens.why: Scammers use hyphens to cram official-sounding words into a domain name to make it look trustworthy. Real organisations keep their web addresses simple.
url_many_hyphens.do: If a domain looks like it was built by joining official-sounding words with hyphens, it is probably fake. Check the real domain of the organisation you are looking for.

url_suspicious_word.title: Suspicious Action Word in Link
url_suspicious_word.what: The link contains words like 'login', 'verify', 'kyc', 'secure', 'update', or 'confirm' — words that suggest you need to take urgent action on a website.
url_suspicious_word.why: Scam websites are designed to mimic the login or verification pages of real banks. They trick you into entering your credentials, which they then steal.
url_suspicious_word.do: Do not go to any website from an unexpected link, no matter how official the URL looks. Always access your bank by typing the address directly.

lookalike_edit_distance.title: This Link Pretends to Be a Real Company
lookalike_edit_distance.what: The website address is almost identical to a well-known brand's real address — just one or two letters changed, swapped, or missing (e.g. 'paytrn.com' instead of 'paytm.com').
lookalike_edit_distance.why: People read quickly and miss small differences. Scammers register these near-identical addresses and build perfect copies of the real website to steal your password and money.
lookalike_edit_distance.do: Always check the exact spelling of any website address. Bookmark official sites so you never mistype them. If you arrived via a link, close the page and go directly.

lookalike_brand_in_domain.title: Brand Name Hidden in a Fake Address
lookalike_brand_in_domain.what: This link contains a real company name (like 'SBI', 'Paytm', or 'HDFC') but it is part of a different, unofficial website address.
lookalike_brand_in_domain.why: Scammers put trusted brand names into fake domains — like 'sbi-kyc-update.in' — to make them look official at first glance. The 'sbi' part is just decoration; the real domain is something else entirely.
lookalike_brand_in_domain.do: The brand name at the START of a link does not mean anything. What matters is the registered domain — the part just before the final extension (.in, .com). Verify on the company's official site.

lookalike_homoglyph.title: Letters Swapped to Look Identical
lookalike_homoglyph.what: This link uses characters that look exactly like real letters but are actually different — like using the number '0' instead of the letter 'o', or '1' instead of 'l'.
lookalike_homoglyph.why: At a glance, 'paypa1.com' looks identical to 'paypal.com'. Scammers register these look-alike domains to fool people who do not scrutinise every character.
lookalike_homoglyph.do: Zoom in and carefully read every character in a suspicious link. When in doubt, do not click — type the known address manually instead.

upi_prefilled_amount.title: QR Code Has a Pre-Filled Payment Amount
upi_prefilled_amount.what: This QR code already has an amount set — so if you scan it with your UPI app, you will be prompted to pay that exact amount automatically.
upi_prefilled_amount.why: Scammers pre-fill amounts in QR codes so you pay without noticing. They might claim you are 'receiving' a refund or cashback, but scanning always SENDS money, never receives it.
upi_prefilled_amount.do: If a QR code has a pre-filled amount, do not scan it unless you are absolutely sure you intend to pay that person. To receive money, you should never need to scan anything.

upi_scam_note.title: Payment Note Contains Scam Words
upi_scam_note.what: The transaction note on this UPI QR contains words like 'refund', 'cashback', 'prize', or 'claim' — used to make a payment look like something coming to you.
upi_scam_note.why: By labelling a payment QR as 'refund' or 'cashback', scammers trick you into thinking you are receiving money when you are actually sending it. The note is just text — it does not change the direction of money.
upi_scam_note.do: Remember: any QR scan = money going OUT of your account. Ignore what the note says. Never scan a QR to receive money.

upi_name_mismatch.title: Payee Name and Address Do Not Match
upi_name_mismatch.what: The name shown in the QR (like 'SBI Customer Care') does not match the UPI payment address (like 'randomuser123@ybl').
upi_name_mismatch.why: Anyone can set any display name in a UPI QR — it is not verified. Scammers use official-sounding names to hide the fact that money is going to a personal or fraudulent account.
upi_name_mismatch.do: Check the actual UPI address (the @handle), not just the display name. If they look unrelated, or the address is a personal-looking one, do not pay.
